chunks: From him, from his father, from Ibn Mahbub, from Abu Hamza al-Thumali, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

Among the Children of Israel there was a judge who judged with the truth. When death approached him, he said to his wife: 'When I die, wash me, shroud me, place me on my bed, and cover my face, for you will not see any defect.' When he died, she did that, and remained for a while. Then she uncovered his face to look at him, and found a worm gnawing his nostril. She was startled by this. When it was night, he came to her in her sleep and said: 'Did what you saw frighten you?' She said: 'Yes, I was indeed frightened.' He said: 'If you were frightened, what you saw was only due to a preference (bias) in your brother Fulan. He came to me with a plaintiff. When they sat before me, I said: O God, make the truth for him and direct the judgment against his opponent.' When they disputed before me, the truth was for him, and I saw that clearly in the judgment, so I directed the judgment for him against his opponent. Thus, the place of my preference was with the concurrence of the truth.
ai.seo_question: What is the story of the judge in the Children of Israel whose bias caused a physical defect after death?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the Shia concept of *hawa* (personal inclination) affecting even the most righteous judges, where a subtle bias toward a specific party led to a minor deviation in justice, manifested physically as a worm in the nostril. It serves as a critical scholarly reminder that judicial integrity requires not only adherence to legal truth but also the purification of the heart from hidden preferences, a theme central to the qualifications of *al-qudat* (judges) in Shia jurisprudence. The narrative underscores the spiritual consequences of even unintentional bias, linking moral purity directly to the validity of one's authority.
